summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct is lawful in Vietnam and has never been criminalised in Vietnamese history. The Penal Code sets the age of consent at 16 without regard to gender or sexual orientation. The 1812 Gia Long Code, Article 332, prohibited prostitution and illicit sexual activity including extra-marital sex, and prosecutions of homosexual conduct could in rare cases be brought under those labels, but pre-colonial enforcement was inconsistent and little to no state action is recorded.

Official hostility has a documented history. In 2002 the Ministry of Labour, Invalids and Social Affairs declared homosexuality a "social evil" comparable to prostitution, gambling and drug use, and promised legislation to combat homosexuality and to arrest same-sex couples. Fines on same-sex marriages were abolished by government decree on 24 September 2013, effective 11 November 2013. The 2015 removal of the same-sex-marriage ban left couples' unions without legal recognition, and same-sex unions were subsequently removed from the list of forbidden acts while conferring no rights.

Legal gender recognition remains unimplemented. The 2015 Civil Code amendment, passed on 24 November 2015 by 282 votes to 84 and effective from January 2017, allows a person who has undergone sex reassignment to register under their preferred sex, but a further implementing bill is required and has not been enacted, so the provision is not fully enforced. Sex reassignment surgery was previously illegal, which pushed transgender Vietnamese to undergo the procedure in Thailand. A draft law protecting transgender people's legal status was expected before the National Assembly by 2020 and never materialised; a recognition draft law was still under consideration as of February 2026, nine years after implementing legislation was first promised for 2017. Under the Law on Citizen Identification effective 1 July 2024, transgender citizens may change their ID card when undergoing gender transition but must present confirmation documents, and the legal effect of that change depends on the gender-affirmation law being passed first.

No Vietnamese law provides discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, according to a Refugee Protection Division country-information request of 30 June 2022 drawing on Freedom House material dated 3 March 2021. Amnesty International's Viet Nam 2025 report found that LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice, in a wider environment in which vaguely worded Penal Code articles 109, 116, 117 and 331 were used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025.

Healthcare access is uneven in practice. A United Nations Viet Nam feature of 30 November 2024 records transgender women reporting routine discrimination at healthcare encounters, including being asked "Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?", heightened scrutiny at appointments, and economic and stigma-driven exposure to physical and sexual violence, with the sharpest risk reported by trans women in northern provinces and ethnic-minority communities. A June 2023 Saigoneer account of four transgender Vietnamese describes respectful treatment from healthcare providers undermined by administrative red tape, the implementing guidance of the November 2015 milestone having stalled. The Health Ministry declared in August 2022 that same-sex attraction and transgender identity are not mental disorders, and Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC of 3 August 2022 outlawed conversion therapy, stating that lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people may not be forced into "treatment" and mandating nationwide communication to medical facilities plus psychological support from people who understand gender identity.

A Lighthouse Vietnam study published in October 2024, "Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in Vietnam", documents the forms these efforts take in the Vietnamese context alongside a data-needs analysis. No law addresses non-consensual medical interventions on intersex people.

Public assembly space narrowed in 2025. Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other Pride events during 2025; the Asia director of Human Rights Watch, Patricia Gossman, described the cancellations as worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, set against Vietnam's long regional reputation for tolerance. LGBTIQ organisations in the country operate openly but under government surveillance.

Detention carries unresolved exposure. In January 2015 the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute proposed to the Ministry of Public Security that homosexual and transgender prisoners be housed separately from the general prison population to protect them from sexual harassment, citing a 2014 survey in which most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails and noting that under the prison infrastructure then in place transgender prisoners could be held only in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, with no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity. The proposal asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome is documented.
tangentialFactors:
Vietnam's Pride movement grew from the country's first gay pride parade in Hanoi on 5 August 2012 to events in around 34 cities and provinces by 2017, with more than 35 held annually in cities including Haiphong, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City and Cần Thơ. Hanoi Pride's fifth edition, 18–24 September 2017, drew thousands against roughly a hundred at the first parade, and the sixth edition in November 2018 saw more than 1,000 participants cycling in support of transgender rights and same-sex marriage. Several of these events were carried on state channels VTV4, VTV6 and VTV9, which makes the 2025 cancellations a change in documented official posture rather than a continuation of the earlier pattern.

Media treatment shifted measurably over two decades. In 2002 publications such as Thế Giới Phụ Nữ and Tiếp thị & Gia đình described homosexuality as a disease and "deviant behavior"; in September 2010 Tuoi Tre Online became the first major state media outlet to state that "homosexuality is normal". The 2013 sitcom My Best Gay Friends was released on YouTube because Vietnamese broadcasters were reluctant to air it.

Public opinion data is favourable relative to the region but does not bear on legal exposure. Pew data from 2023 puts support for same-sex marriage at 79% among 18–34-year-olds and 57% among those aged 35 and above. A 2007 poll of 300 junior-high and high-school pupils at Ho Chi Minh City Pedagogical University found 80% answered "no" to the question "Is homosexuality bad?".

Adjacent protections exist outside the gender-identity framework. In 2006 the government enacted legislation protecting people infected with HIV and people living with AIDS from discrimination, and healthcare is provided free to all Vietnamese citizens. Amnesty International's 2025 report places the absence of LGBTI protections alongside wider repression, including proposed press-law rules requiring disclosure of sources, while Viet Nam was re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council for a term running to 2028.
localsOnly:
Discrimination and violence in education are documented for resident students. A 2015 study found around 44% of Vietnamese LGBT students aged 14–22 faced stigma, discrimination and violence because of their identities. A 2014 USAID report showed 54% of LGBT students saying their school was not safe, with many dropping out; among those who experienced violence, one third thought about committing suicide and half of those attempted it. The same period's figures record that 85% of transgender students dropped out because of assault and bullying. A 2015 UNESCO study found 19% of students perceived bullying against LGBT students as "harmless", and 70% of Hanoi parents said they would not allow their children to talk to gay students, with some believing conversion therapy could "cure" LGBT children.

LGBTIQ organisations operate openly in Vietnam but under government surveillance, a condition that shapes resident organising more than short-term visits. The Health Ministry's August 2022 position that homosexuality, bisexuality and transgender identity are not illnesses, and Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC of 3 August 2022, bind medical facilities nationwide and direct that psychological support be provided by people with an understanding of gender identity.

For residents, the practical barrier to legal gender recognition is administrative rather than statutory: the November 2015 Civil Code milestone allowed people who changed gender to apply for a civil-status change and set out the framework for recognition, but implementing guidance stalled and policy gaps persist. Under the Law on Citizen Identification effective 1 July 2024, an ID card change on gender transition requires confirmation documents and awaits the gender-affirmation law. Health care is free to all Vietnamese citizens, and the 2006 statute protects people living with HIV from discrimination.

Prison conditions for transgender detainees remain as described in the January 2015 proposal: with no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity, transgender prisoners could be held only in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population. No enacted outcome of that proposal is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the gender-affirmation law will be enacted is unresolved in this record. A recognition draft law was still under consideration as of February 2026, and no source here reports a vote, a date for one, or a rejection.

The January 2015 proposal to house homosexual and transgender prisoners separately has no documented enacted outcome. Whether any pilot, directive or subsequent regulation followed is not sourced, and the current housing practice for transgender detainees in Vietnamese prisons is not stated by any source in this inventory.

Enforcement of Dispatch No. 4132/BYT-PC is not sourced. The inventory records the dispatch's content and its mandated communications work but contains no compliance data, complaint records or evidence of penalties against practitioners who continue conversion efforts; the October 2024 Lighthouse Vietnam study documents that such efforts occur, without a national prevalence figure.

No trans-specific homicide or violence figure with a denominator appears in this inventory, so no comparison against Vietnam's general homicide rate can be made here. The violence risk described by the UN feature of 30 November 2024 is qualitative and self-reported, not a measured rate.

The discrimination finding rests on a Refugee Protection Division country-information request of 30 June 2022 relaying Freedom House material dated 3 March 2021; no later comprehensive legal survey of sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination provisions is available in this record. Whether any subordinate regulation since 2021 supplies such protection is not sourced.

The scope of the 2025 Pride cancellations beyond Ho Chi Minh City and the five additional events reported is not sourced, and no source here states whether those events were prohibited, postponed or withdrawn by organisers.
